summary: This experimental document describes a signal-free mechanism for LISP multicast. When multicast sites are connected over a core that has no native multicast, it lets multicast traffic still be delivered between sites. It avoids the usual signaling to set up group membership.

plainLanguage.summary: If a school cannot make a loudspeaker across town, it can mail copies instead. This uses copies sent to the right places without long setup messages.

questions: how does signal-free lisp multicast work
how to run multicast over lisp without native core multicast
how are receivers registered in lisp
subtitle: Deliver multicast traffic across LISP sites without native multicast in the core.

tldr.problem: LISP sites (networks using Locator/ID Separation Protocol) want to join their multicast trees together, but most internet cores do not support multicast. Traditional solutions require extending multicast signaling (PIM) across the LISP overlay or explicit signaling between endpoints, creating signaling overhead.
tldr.mechanism: Instead of signaling, receiver sites register their addresses in the LISP mapping database as having multicast receivers. Source sites query the mapping database to find all receiver endpoints, then replicate and encapsulate multicast packets as unicast tunnels to each receiver. The mapping database acts as a multicast receiver registry.
tldr.outcome: Multicast traffic flows between LISP sites over a multicast-free core, with minimal signaling overhead. The mechanism is 'signal-free' because group membership is discovered via the mapping database rather than explicit join messages.

facts.label: RLE level values
facts.value: 128 for receivers, configurable for RTR levels

today: RFC 8378 is an Experimental specification that defines how LISP-based multicast can operate without native multicast in the core network. It has been tested by operators deploying LISP for carrier networks and remains in experimental status as deployment experience is gathered.

sections.title: Multicast Over LISP Without Core Multicast
sections.content:
LISP separates endpoint identifiers (EIDs) from routing locators (RLOCs). Hosts at LISP sites send traffic to EID addresses; the LISP mapping system routes packets based on RLOC addresses in the core.

Multicast sources and receivers at different LISP sites want multicast traffic to reach all receivers, but most internet backbones do not run multicast. The RFC describes a way to tunnel multicast between sites using the LISP infrastructure without requiring multicast in the core.

The approach avoids extending PIM (Protocol Independent Multicast) signaling across the overlay and avoids direct signaling between source and receiver sites. Instead, receiver sites register themselves in the mapping system, and source sites query the mapping system to find all receivers for a (source, group) pair, then replicate and unicast-encapsulate the traffic to each receiver.
sections.plainLanguage: Towns have their own post offices and mail sorters. Instead of making the whole road carry broadcasts, the sender gets a list of sorters from the central office and sends copies there.

sections.title: Receiver and Source Site Procedures
sections.content:
The mechanism splits into three procedures: receiver-site operations, source-site operations, and LISP mapping system notifications.

At receiver sites, hosts join multicast groups locally using IGMP or PIM. The Receiver-ETR (the LISP exit router at the receiver site) detects these joins. It then registers its locator (RLOC) in the LISP mapping database as a receiver for the (source, group) multicast tuple, using the Multicast Info and RLE (Replication List Entry) LCAF types defined in RFC 8060.

The mapping system (Map-Servers) merge registrations from multiple receiver ETRs for the same (source, group) pair into a single replication list. When a source site needs the replication list, it sends a Map-Request for the (source, group) tuple. The Map-Server responds with a Map-Reply containing all receiver RLOCs.

At source sites, the source sends multicast packets to the multicast group address. A local multicast tree (built via PIM) carries the packet to the Source-ITR. The Source-ITR queries the mapping system for the (source, group) replication list, caches it, and then replicates the packet to each RLOC on the list, unicast-encapsulating each copy.
sections.plainLanguage: Listeners tell their local sorter they want the mail. The sorter writes their address in the central notebook. The sender asks the central office for all listeners, gets the list, makes copies, and mails one to each listener.

sections.title: LISP Message Encoding and Procedures
sections.content:
All signaling uses existing LISP message types (Map-Request, Map-Reply, Map-Register) with new encoding. Multicast (source, group) pairs are encoded using the Multicast Info LCAF Type, and receiver locator lists use the RLE LCAF Type. Both are defined in RFC 8060.

Receiver-ETRs send Map-Register messages with the merge-request bit set to 1, asking the Map-Server to merge multiple registrations from different sites. They set want-map-notify to 0 (no per-change notifications) and proxy-reply to 1 (Map-Server proxies replies to Map-Requests). The RLE entry contains the ETR's locator(s) with a level value of 128, indicating a receiver endpoint.

Source-ITRs register their unicast source address (S-prefix) with the mapping system and set want-map-notify to 1 so they receive Map-Notify messages when the receiver list changes. Map-Notify messages from the Map-Server inform the source site of new receivers for each (source, group), triggering local multicast tree building (via PIM joins) if needed.
sections.plainLanguage: The notebooks use a special format for group addresses. Listeners mark themselves as level 128 (receivers). Senders ask for updates whenever the list changes.

sections.title: Source-Specific and Any-Source Multicast
sections.content:
Source-Specific Multicast (SSM) is simpler than Any-Source Multicast (ASM). In SSM, the source IP is known, so the source site can register the source address with the mapping system to receive Map-Notify messages. When a source directly connects to the Source-ITR, no local multicast tree building is required; the source sends directly to the ITR, which replicates to all registered receivers.

ASM requires a Rendezvous Point (RP) that sources initially register with and receivers join. The RFC suggests running ASM independently within each LISP site. Each site has its own RP (or multiple RPs). Receiver sites register their ETR as an RP and register (*,G) (any source for group G) entries. When a source appears, it sends PIM Register messages to its local RP. The source-site ITR then registers the new (source, group) pair with the mapping system and receives Map-Notify messages about receivers. A source-site ITR that is also the RP registers (S-prefix, G) entries.
sections.plainLanguage: If you know who is sending, you ask the office to tell you each time a listener joins. If anyone can send, each town runs its own meeting coordinator who collects join messages.

sections.title: Reducing Head-End Replication Load
sections.content:
Replication Engineering applies the signal-free mechanism to build a hierarchy of replicating routers (RTRs) that reduce the load on the source-site ITR. Instead of the ITR replicating to every receiver site, it replicates to a layer of level-0 RTRs. Those RTRs in turn replicate to level-1 RTRs, and so on, creating a replication tree. The mapping system encodes level values in the RLE LCAF type so routers know which level to replicate to.

When an ITR receives a Map-Reply with multiple RLOC-records for different levels, it can choose between a 'complete-format' view (showing both ETRs and RTRs) and a 'filtered-format' view (showing only RTRs). The policy shift from ITR-driven replication to Map-Server-driven policy is operator-configurable.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of the sender making millions of copies, it makes copies for a few regional offices, which make copies for their local offices, and so on.

sections.title: Multihoming and Load Balancing
sections.content:
When multiple ITRs exist at a source site, only one should replicate packets to avoid duplicates. The RFC specifies that the PIM Designated Router (DR) or IGMP querier on the source LAN is responsible for replication; other ITRs silently drop the packet. Similar rules apply for multiple ETRs at a receiver site: the PIM DR or IGMP querier sends the Map-Register.

An ETR can register multiple RLOCs for path redundancy, using the Explicit Locator Path (ELP) LCAF Type nested in the RLE. An ITR probes reachability to each RLOC and chooses a working one. Multiple receiver sites can share the same multicast group; the mapping system merges all their RLOCs into one replication list.
sections.plainLanguage: When a town has two mail sorters, one is picked to listen and register. When an office has multiple addresses, the sender picks the one that works.
